title: Accommodate audience and context needs in oral communication

lessons.title: Knowing your audience and purpose
lessons.html:
Communication depends on who is listening

As a team leader in a fruit packhouse, a poultry plant or a seed operation, you speak to many different audiences in one day: packers on the line, the quality controller, a truck driver, the production manager, an auditor, a visiting buyer. The same message must be delivered differently to each of them. Accommodating your audience means choosing words, tone, length and examples that suit the listener and the situation.

Analyse the audience

  • Knowledge: How much do they already know? A new seasonal packer needs basic explanations; a quality manager wants technical detail.
  • Language: What languages do they understand best? Should you use isiZulu, Sesotho, Afrikaans or English, or a mix with translation?
  • Relationship: Are they your team, your manager, a customer or an official? This affects how formal you should be.
  • Attitude: Are they likely to be interested, worried, resistant or rushed?
  • Size: one person, a small team or a large group at a shift briefing?

Clarify your purpose

PurposeExample
To informTelling the team that a new export market requires different carton labels
To instructExplaining the new hand-wash procedure
To persuadeConvincing management to replace a worn grading belt
To negotiateAgreeing overtime arrangements for peak season
To build relationshipsWelcoming a visiting buyer

Register and tone

Register is the level of formality. With your team at a toolbox talk, a friendly, direct register works. In a meeting with an auditor, use a formal, precise register and correct terminology. Tone should always remain respectful. Avoid slang, sarcasm and jokes that might offend, especially across cultures.

lessons.title: Adapting your message and delivery
lessons.html:
Shaping the message

Structure

Most work talks follow a simple structure:

  1. Opening: greet, state the topic and why it matters.
  2. Body: main points in logical order, with examples.
  3. Close: summarise, state the action needed, and invite questions.

Choosing words

  • Use plain language for general audiences: 'wash your hands for at least 20 seconds' rather than 'ensure adequate hand hygiene duration'.
  • Explain technical terms the first time: 'Brix, which is the sugar content of the fruit'.
  • Use concrete examples from the workplace, such as a photo of a correctly packed carton.
  • With mixed-language teams, keep sentences short, repeat key points, and ask a trusted team member to translate if needed.

Non-verbal communication

Your body language, eye contact, facial expression and gestures support or undermine your words. Stand where everyone can see and hear you. Make eye contact around the group. Use gestures to demonstrate. Be aware that cultural norms differ; for example, some people show respect by avoiding direct eye contact with seniors.

Voice

Vary your pace, volume and tone. Slow down for important instructions. In noisy areas such as near a grader or plucker, move the group to a quieter spot rather than shouting.

Using visual aids

Flipcharts, samples, photographs and simple charts help listeners understand, particularly when language is a barrier. Show a defective fruit sample alongside a good one rather than describing defects only in words.

Telephone and radio

Without visual cues, you must be extra clear. Identify yourself, state the purpose, speak clearly, confirm details by repeating them, and end by agreeing actions. On two-way radios, keep messages short and follow your site's radio procedure.

lessons.title: Interactive communication: meetings, feedback and conflict
lessons.html:
Two-way communication

Good oral communication is not only speaking; it is interaction. You must listen, check understanding and respond to what others say.

Active listening

  • Give full attention and stop other tasks.
  • Show you are listening: nod, make brief comments such as 'I see'.
  • Paraphrase: 'So you are saying the cold room door is not closing properly at night?'
  • Ask open questions to find out more: 'What happened next?'
  • Ask closed questions to confirm facts: 'Was it at 22:00?'

Participating in meetings

In production or safety meetings:

  • Prepare your points and figures beforehand.
  • Keep contributions brief and relevant.
  • Support views with facts: 'We had 14 rejected pallets last week due to label errors.'
  • Disagree politely and focus on the issue, not the person.
  • Make sure decisions and responsibilities are clear before the meeting ends.

Giving and receiving feedback

When giving feedback to a team member, be specific, timely and balanced. Describe the behaviour and its effect, then agree what to do: 'Today three cartons were underweight because the scale was not zeroed. Please check the scale at the start of each pallet.' When receiving feedback, listen without becoming defensive, ask for examples and thank the person.

Handling sensitive or difficult conversations

Some conversations need extra care: a worker who is grieving, a performance problem, or a complaint from a customer. Choose a private place, stay calm, listen first, show empathy and keep to facts. If emotions run high, suggest a short break and continue later.

Respecting diversity

South African workplaces bring together many cultures, languages, ages and genders. Use respectful forms of address, avoid stereotypes and be patient with people speaking in a second or third language.

Key points

  • Analyse your audience's knowledge, language, relationship and attitude.
  • Match your register and tone to the audience and context.
  • Structure talks with an opening, body and close with clear action.
  • Use plain language, examples and visual aids to overcome barriers.
  • Listen actively, paraphrase and give specific, balanced feedback.
